Your hand settles on Corm's shoulder, the holy water falls in a fine silver line over his scarred arm, and the warding settles on him like a cloak. "Steady, old friend," you say, and begin.

The warding on Corm flickers as the heartstone pulses hot and cold. Hild has drawn her crossbow but not raised it, and Garrick has fitted an arrow at the bend and stands waiting for your word.

You are twenty names from the end, with Brenn's still to speak. The sleeper is frightened, not angry, and the rite is not broken yet. It needs a steady voice. What does Brun do?

The warding takes hold of Corm like a thin, clean frost, and his shoulders ease under your touch. You open the book and begin.

input.add_to_description: Dawn Day 4: Rite performed (Religion 18). Sleeper released with mercy; door opened by itself. The sixty were found at rest in the lower gallery, Brenn holding the stone-spirit's 'hand' (a hand-shaped boulder). Hild and Corm will bring up the dead for burial. Quest essentially complete; 200 XP awarded.

entries.text: notebook: updated Mend the Hearthdeep Seal

The warding light settles over Corm like a thin gold mantle, and he breathes out slowly. Then you begin.

The invocation first, in Father Dorrin's cadence, and the iron grows warm under your holy symbol. Then the names, one by one, in the captain's order. You say each as if it were kin. The heartstone brightens with every one, and the hum in your teeth shifts from a drone to something almost like a voice, rising and falling with each name, as if it were listening and counting.

At the fortieth the floor trembles, and Hild's hand finds Garrick's sleeve. At the fiftieth the iron bands ring like a struck bell. Corm's arm shakes but he does not move it. You do not stop. You say the fifty-ninth, and then the last, plainly, with all the love in you: "Brenn Ironvein."

Silence. Then the stone gives a long, low sigh, like a great animal lying down, and the sweet smell drains out of the air as if drawn through a sieve. The three strokes on the door fade from the iron one after another. The heartstone's glow goes soft as dawn, and the door swings inward on its own, without a sound.

Beyond is a long gallery of pale dust, and there is no horror in it. The sixty lie at rest along both walls, laid in rows with their hands folded, as though someone had tended them for forty winters. At the far end, a boulder the size of a cart sits like a bowed head, and one great hand-shaped spur of it rests open on the floor. Brenn lies against it, his own hand in its palm.

Hild makes a sound you have never heard from her, and goes down the gallery alone. Corm sinks to his knees, his arm free at last, and weeps without hiding it.

You have earned 200 XP, reaching 900, enough for level 3. The rite is done, the sleeper at peace, and the dead can go home.

When you are ready, we can take your level. What does Brun do first?

The sleeper, the hold's own stone-heart, was released with mercy; its grief ebbed out of the mountain and the slope grew still. The door opened on the lower gallery: the sixty lay at rest in a ring, as if sleeping, Brenn among them holding the sleeper's hollow stone. The ward settles over Corm like frost, and his grip on the stone steadies. You open Father Dorrin's book, lay your holy symbol on the iron, and begin.

The Morninglord's invocation comes first, and the heartstone answers it with a faint warmth. Then the names, one by one, slow and even, each set down like a stone in a cairn. Somewhere around the twentieth the hum rises, not in anger but in attention, as if something vast has turned its head. By the fortieth the iron beneath your hand is trembling like a held breath. Hild's lips move silently with every name. Corm's eyes are shut and his face wet.

You say Brenn Ironvein last, and your voice does not break.

The door does not crash open. It sighs. The iron bands loosen, the stone seam parts, and a long, tired breath rolls out of the dark that smells of cold rain on rock and nothing else. Beyond that, deeper in the hills, a ring of small lamps that burn without oil, the Deepwatch, and a sense, like a hand on your shoulder, that someone there has been waiting for you by name.

Maren is quiet for a dozen paces, and then she begins, and does not stop for a long while.

Your mother, she says, loved honeyed barley cakes and burnt the edges on purpose, and would fight anyone who tried to pare them. She sang the miners' counting-song, "Seven Lamps," and sang it badly, and was happy to be told so. In every shaft she surveyed she chalked a tiny sun on the wall at the survey's end, so that whoever came next would know a friend had been there. "She named you for the old captain, Brunhilde, who held the lower gate at the first fall," Maren says. "She said a name should be heavy enough to stand on."

The Deepwatch itself, she tells you, is a hall cut into the face of a hill, its great doors carved with the hammer and three lines. Every night a ring of lamps is lit along the ridge, one for each warden living. "Many are dark now," she says. "But we light them all the same, and the dark ones too, with a small pebble in the lamp, so we know whose place it is."

You walk with that for a while. Somewhere in the telling you notice, tucked in the back cover of Father Dorrin's prayer book, two folded letters sealed with wardens' wax and addressed in his cramped hand to the Deepwatch. You had not seen them before. You leave them sealed, for the moment, and Maren, glancing at them, only nods once, as if she has been expecting them.

At dusk the waymark-hut comes into view on the saddle, a squat dry-stone shelter with a turf roof, a hearth, and a stack of old peat. You cook, as you promised: oatcakes, dried apple, and a broth of salt pork and barley from Garrick's stores, which he eats in silence and then, unexpectedly, praises with a single word. The wind rises and the stars come out thick over the hills.

You are at full strength, with three spell slots and Channel Divinity ready. The Deepwatch lies a day and a half ahead. What does Brun do?

entries.text:
Maren is quiet for the first hundred paces, and you let her be. Then, as the wind drops in the lee of a ridge, she begins.

The Deepwatch, she says, is cut into a cliff of black granite above a still lake, so dark that the stars lie in it at night. Its gate is called the Quiet Door, because the wardens hold that a mine's first lesson is to listen. Inside lies the Lamp-Gallery, a long vaulted hall hung with ten thousand small lamps, one for every warden living or lost, and on certain nights the keepers walk its length and trim each wick by hand. "Your mother's lamp is still lit," she says. "We never let it go out. Yours was lit the day you were born. Dorrin did not know that."

Then the small things, as you asked. Sigrun hoarded honey-oatcakes in her boots as a girl, and her feet smelled of them for a year. She hummed a work-song called "Lamp and Line" and always sang the second verse off-key, on purpose, to annoy the choirmaster. She chalked her surveys across the hall's flagstones until she was made to scrub them, and then chalked them again. She named every shaft she ever mapped after a bird. "Wren Deep. Kestrel Cut. The one that took her was a small one. She called it Dipper."

You laugh at the oatcakes, and then you do not, and Maren pretends not to see. She hums a line of the song for you, flat and cracked, and you find that you know the tune after all. You have been humming it over washing-up your whole life.

The light goes long and amber. By seven the waymark-hut appears on its saddle: a squat roundhouse of dry-laid stone with a turf roof and the wardens' sign carved over the lintel. line:
Brun falls into step beside Maren and shortens her stride to match. "Aunt Maren, while we walk, would you tell me about the Deepwatch itself, and about my mother as a girl? I'd like to hear the small things, like what she liked to eat and what songs she sang."

She glances ahead at Garrick and adds, "Garrick, thank you for the ford and the sheep trail. At the waymark-hut tonight I'll cook, since you've done the hard work all day."

input.add_to_description: Told by Maren on the road (Day 5): as a girl Sigrun hoarded charcoal stubs and drew maps on the hall walls until the wardens gave her a slate; loved barley-honey cakes and burned them every time she baked; sang a work-song about a lamp-lighter called 'Slow Tam' off-key and loudly; was afraid of nothing underground and terrified of geese.

Described by Maren on the road: carved into the north face of a great grey tor, with a hall of lamps, a records vault called the Long Shelf, and a gate whose lintel reads the same as the Hearthdeep door: 'What the hold keeps, the hold remembers.' Fewer than a hundred wardens' kin remain.

entries.text: time: 3 hours 30 minutes later: Day 5, 5:59 PM

Maren is quiet for a dozen paces, and then she begins, and you realize you have asked the one question she has wanted for years to be asked.

"Your mother kept charcoal in her pockets," she says. "Stubs of it, everywhere. By six she had drawn a map of the whole hall on the corridor wall, every stair and cupboard, and the wardens were so angry and so impressed that they gave her a slate to keep her off the stone." The staff keeps its beat. "She baked barley-honey cakes, and she burned every one. She ate them anyway, and said the black was where the flavor was. She sang a work-song about a lamp-lighter named Slow Tam, loudly and badly, and she would not be told she was off-key."

You laugh before you can stop yourself, and then your eyes sting. Maren nods as if that is exactly right.

"She was afraid of nothing underground. Not the dark, not the deep seams, not a roof that groaned. But she was terrified of geese." Her mouth twitches. "A gander chased her across the whole mill-yard once, and she climbed a cart and screamed until the miller's wife came out with a broom."

Of the Deepwatch itself she tells you in smaller pieces, between breaths on the climbs. It is cut into the north face of a great grey tor, with a hall of lamps that are never let go out, and a records vault the wardens call the Long Shelf. The gate's lintel carries the same words as the Hearthdeep door, *What the hold keeps, the hold remembers.* There are fewer than a hundred of the wardens' kin left there now.

Garrick says almost nothing, but twice you catch him slowing his pace to let Maren catch up, pretending to study the ground.

At six the waymark-hut comes into view on the saddle, a low, turf-roofed stone shelter with a hearth, a woodstack under a lean-to, and a cairn at the door. The wind has picked up and the sky is going coppery in the west. You keep your word and cook: oatcakes toasted on the hearthstone, a pot of barley and dried apple stewed with the last of the salt pork, and a pinch of the innkeeper's wife's herbs. Garrick eats two bowls without comment, which from him is a speech.

One thing for the record: your sheet now lists two letters among your belongings, Father Dorrin's hidden letters to the Deepwatch, which you have not yet opened or described. I do not want to invent what is in them for you. If you take them out tonight, tell me what you do.

It is evening, at the saddle, with the hut warm and the stars coming out. You have three spell slots, Channel Divinity, and a day and a half of road left. What does Brun do?

There are more lamps than there are wardens now. We do not put them out." She is quiet a moment. "It has a small school, for the children of the wardens. features: Darkvision: You have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You cannot discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.
Dwarven Resilience: You have advantage on saving throws against poison, and you have resistance against poison damage.

Stonecunning: Whenever you make an Intelligence (History) check related to the origin of stonework, you are considered proficient in the History skill and add double your proficiency bonus to the check, instead of your normal proficiency bonus.
Dwarven Combat Training: You have proficiency with the battleaxe, handaxe, light hammer, and warhammer.
Tool Proficiency: You gain proficiency with the artisan's tools of your choice: smith's tools, brewer's supplies, or mason's tools.
Dwarven Toughness: Your hit point maximum increases by 1, and it increases by 1 every time you gain a level.

Divine Domain: Choose one domain related to your deity, such as Life. Each domain is detailed at the end of the class description, and each one provides examples of gods associated with it. Your choice grants you domain spells and other features when you choose it at 1st level. It also grants you additional ways to use Channel Divinity when you gain that feature at 2nd level, and additional benefits at 6th, 8th, and 17th levels.

Domain Spells: Each domain has a list of spells--its domain spells--that you gain at the cleric levels noted in the domain description. Once you gain a domain spell, you always have it prepared, and it doesn't count against the number of spells you can prepare each day. If you have a domain spell that doesn't appear on the cleric spell list, the spell is nonetheless a cleric spell for you.
Bonus Proficiency: When you choose this domain at 1st level, you gain proficiency with heavy armor.

Disciple of Life: Also starting at 1st level, your healing spells are more effective. Whenever you use a spell of 1st level or higher to restore hit points to a creature, the creature regains additional hit points equal to 2 + the spell's level.

Channel Divinity (1/rest): At 2nd level, you gain the ability to channel divine energy directly from your deity, using that energy to fuel magical effects. You start with two such effects: Turn Undead and an effect determined by your domain. Some domains grant you additional effects as you advance in levels, as noted in the domain description. When you use your Channel Divinity, you choose which effect to create. You must then finish a short or long rest to use your Channel Divinity again. Some Channel Divinity effects require saving throws. When you use such an effect from this class, the DC equals your cleric spell save DC. Beginning at 6th level, you can use your Channel Divinity twice between rests, and beginning at 18th level, you can use it three times between rests. When you finish a short or long rest, you regain your expended uses.

Channel Divinity: Turn Undead: As an action, you present your holy symbol and speak a prayer censuring the undead. Each undead that can see or hear you within 30 feet of you must make a Wisdom saving throw. If the creature fails its saving throw, it is turned for 1 minute or until it takes any damage. A turned creature must spend its turns trying to move as far away from you as it can, and it can't willingly move to a space within 30 feet of you. It also can't take reactions. For its action, it can use only the Dash action or try to escape from an effect that prevents it from moving. If there's nowhere to move, the creature can use the Dodge action.

Channel Divinity: Preserve Life: Starting at 2nd level, you can use your Channel Divinity to heal the badly injured. As an action, you present your holy symbol and evoke healing energy that can restore a number of hit points equal to five times your cleric level. Choose any creatures within 30 feet of you, and divide those hit points among them. This feature can restore a creature to no more than half of its hit point maximum. You can't use this feature on an undead or a construct. At level 2: 10 hit points to divide.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

line:
Brun squares her shoulders, wipes the rain from her face, and calls up to the sentry in clear Dwarvish, "I'm Brunhilde Stonehearth, Sigrun's daughter, raised by Father Dorrin Ashbeard. I carry a copy of the Hearthdeep warden-captain's ledger, and I've come home."

She keeps one hand on Maren's arm and glances at Garrick. "Stay close, friend. You're with me, and you're welcome here."

input.description: Captain of the Deepwatch. Stern, iron-bearded, Maren's rival of forty years and closest friend. Disapproved of Sigrun's marriage to a non-warden lamp-maker. Meets Brun at the gate hall on the night of Day 6.

input.add_to_description: Day 6 evening: Brun named herself at the gate and showed the ledger copy. The sentry opened the doors; Torvald Greycairn waits in the gate hall. Brun's pack also holds two sealed letters from Father Dorrin to the Deepwatch, unsent, found tucked in the prayer book's binding (unread by Brun yet).

entries.text:
Your voice rings up the cliff face and the sentry goes quiet. The rain drums on your shoulders and the lamps on either side of the gate gutter and steady.

"The ledger," the sentry calls. "Show it."

You dig into your pack and lift out Corm's ledger in its dry cloth. Your fingers close on something else too, tucked deep in the binding of Father Dorrin's prayer book, where you never felt it before: two small folded letters sealed with the Morninglord's sun, one marked *Torvald* and one *Brun, when she is ready*. You do not read them. You hold the ledger up to the lamplight instead, and the sentry looks long at the hammer-and-three-lines on its cover.

Then the sentry is gone from the wall, and somewhere inside a great bar slides back. The bronze doors swing inward without a sound, and warm light spills over the wet stone.

The gate hall is vast and low-vaulted, hung with a hundred lamps that burn without smoke. Wardens in hooded cloaks line the walls, some with spears grounded, some simply watching. At the far end, before a stair that climbs into the mountain, stands a dwarf with an iron-grey beard braided to his belt and a captain's chain across his chest. He is very still. He looks at Maren first and says only, "You are late, old woman." Then his eyes find you, and go to your chin, and stay there.

"You have her face," Torvald Greycairn says at last, his voice rough as a quarry. "I told myself it was a lie, that Dorrin had hidden you for good reason. I did not believe I would live to see it." He steps forward, and the wardens along the walls bow their heads one by one, though he has not asked it.

"Welcome home, Brunhilde Stonehearth. The Hall of Names is lit. Will you eat first, or read first?"

Garrick shifts at your shoulder, a stranger under that vaulted roof, and the letters are warm against your ribs.

What does Brun do?

sheet.name: Brunhilde Stonehearth
sheet.opening: Brunhilde "Brun" Stonehearth, a stocky Hill Dwarf cleric of the Morninglord (Life domain), auburn braid threaded with brass beads, dented but polished chain mail, warhammer worn smooth at the grip, carries the prayer book of her late foster-father figure, Father Dorrin Ashbeard, the old priest who found her as a half-starved orphan in a collapsed mine shaft outside a hill-hold and raised her in his small shrine. She is optimistic, tries to find common ground even between fierce enemies, is suspicious of strangers, and wants to repay the mercy she was shown by walking into danger to keep others alive (ideal: Charity). Opening: it is late afternoon and Brun has just arrived at a rain-soaked crossroads waystation on a mountain road, a squat stone inn and shrine-lean-to shared by travelers, having come down from the hills to carry Father Dorrin's blessing to those in need. A fresh rockslide has just buried part of the road beyond the station, and muffled tapping and a faint cry for help are coming from beneath the stones: a wagon of travelers (a wounded merchant, a child, and a mule-driver) is trapped, and a group of wary, mismatched strangers (a nervous caravan guard, a sullen hunter, and the innkeeper) is arguing over whether it is safe to dig or whether the whole slope will come down. The hurt need a healer now, and the strangers need someone to pull them together before the mountain moves again. Brun, who knows exactly what it is to be trapped under stone and found, is the one they turn to. Her Stonecunning and Smith's Tools may help read the unstable rock and shore it up; her spells (Healing Word, Cure Wounds, Bless, Sanctuary) may keep people alive. Keep the backstory true: Father Dorrin raised her long ago and she carries his book; nothing about it is recent or lost.
